title: Religious Young Men Are Happier, Healthier, and More Successful
author: Ken Burchfiel
summary: Ken Burchfiel uses the April 2025 IFS Young Men's Survey and General Social Survey data to compare young men aged 18 to 29 by religious attendance. Weekly attenders are far more likely to be married, very happy, find life meaningful, hold a bachelor's degree or trade qualification, and have three or more close friends, and are less likely to report poor mental health or loneliness. The pattern challenges the assumption that college secularizes men into worse outcomes, since religious men are more likely to hold degrees. He notes that only 18 percent of young men attend weekly and that attendance has fallen since the 1990s. Burchfiel is careful to flag that the survey is a single snapshot that cannot prove causation, and that the article does not urge men to become religious for worldly benefit. The piece is a data-driven contribution to the debate about the struggles of young men.
points: Forty-one percent of religious young men say they are very happy versus 24 percent of secular men, and secular men are more than twice as likely to report fair or poor mental health.
Religious young men are more, not less, likely to hold a bachelor's degree (46 percent against 16 percent of secular men), contradicting the idea that higher education and faith are opposed.
Weekly attenders have more close friends and less loneliness, and the nature of congregational friendships may matter beyond their number.
Only 18 percent of men aged 18 to 29 attend services weekly, and attendance is lower now than in the 1970s to 1990s.
The author cautions that the data is correlational and that faith should not be pitched merely as a route to success.
quotes: Given these social conditions, it’s not surprising that 42% of young men feel like a failure. The story, however, is brighter for young men who attend religious services at least once a week.

For instance, 41% of religious men consider themselves “very happy” compared to just 24% of secular men. Secular men are also more than twice as likely to report fair or poor mental health (35%) as religious men (15%).
Interestingly, our survey shows the opposite: Religious young men are far more likely (46%) to have a bachelor’s degree than nominal (29%) and secular men (16%).
Those who attend services weekly are more likely to have three or more close friends (68%) than those who rarely or never attend services (52%).
Thus, the nature of religious friendships, and not just their quantity, may play an important role in congregants’ improved well-being.
However, only a minority (18%) of men ages 18 to 29 visit a house of worship this frequently. The majority, 53%, attend less than once a year or not at all.
Our young men’s survey data comes from a single point in time, so these results do not prove that religious attendance itself increases or decreases the likelihood of various outcomes.
In addition, this article does not intend to suggest that young men should become religious simply to have a better chance of success and well-being in life.
